items.stem: Which term describes the view that sociology should use the methods of the natural sciences to discover objective, measurable social facts and laws?
items.answer: Positivism
items.markingKey: Positivism: the view that sociology should use the methods of the natural sciences to discover objective, measurable social facts and laws. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “objectivity”? Give one example.
items.answer: Studying society without letting personal values or bias influence the research. Example: using a standardised questionnaire to avoid influencing answers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (studying society without letting personal values or bias influence the research); 1 mark for a relevant example such as using a standardised questionnaire to avoid influencing answers. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “social facts” and “quantitative data”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Social facts: Durkheim’s term for social phenomena that exist outside individuals and constrain their behaviour (e.g. suicide rates, laws and religious norms). Quantitative data: data in numerical form that can be counted and analysed statistically (e.g. the percentage of respondents who agree with a statement).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Mateo, a researcher in Riyadh, sends a questionnaire with 30 closed questions to 2,000 households to find out whether income affects voting. Suggest how an interpretivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: social reality is constructed through the meanings people give to their actions, so researchers must use qualitative methods such as unstructured interviews and participant observation to achieve verstehen and valid data (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist lives with a group of street children in Bangkok for nine months to understand how they see their own lives. Explain how an interpretivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: social reality is constructed through the meanings people give to their actions, so researchers must use qualitative methods such as unstructured interviews and participant observation to achieve verstehen and valid data (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Leila, a researcher in Toronto, sends a questionnaire with 30 closed questions to 2,000 households to find out whether income affects voting. Explain how positivist and feminist sociologists might differ in the way they evaluate this research.
items.answer: Positivism: sociology should study society scientifically, using quantitative, reliable methods such as questionnaires and official statistics to discover social facts, correlations and causes; the researcher should remain objective and detached (Comte, Durkheim). Feminism: research has often ignored women’s experiences; feminist researchers prefer non-hierarchical, qualitative methods that give women a voice and take account of power relationships in research (Oakley).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) to research the experiences of homeless people in Mumbai.
items.answer: Strengths: they show how people themselves understood their experiences; they give an insight into people’s feelings and meanings in their own words, so validity can be high. Limitations: their meaning must be interpreted by the researcher, which may introduce bias; they may not be authentic or credible; the writer may exaggerate or present themselves favourably. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of homeless people in Mumbai but best combined with another method such as field experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of non-participant observation for studying why some young people leave school early.
items.answer: Strengths: children can be observed in classrooms or playgrounds without having to answer questions; a structured observation schedule allows behaviour to be counted and compared, improving reliability. Limitations: the researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it; observation schedules impose the researcher’s categories on behaviour. Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why some young people leave school early but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that sociology should use the methods of the natural sciences to discover objective, measurable social facts and laws?
items.answer: Positivism
items.markingKey: Positivism: the view that sociology should use the methods of the natural sciences to discover objective, measurable social facts and laws. [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying the experiences of homeless people in Kathmandu.
items.answer: Strengths: anonymity may encourage respondents to admit sensitive or embarrassing behaviour they would not reveal face to face; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of homeless people in Kathmandu but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes the extent to which research gives a true and accurate picture of what it claims to measure?
items.answer: Validity
items.markingKey: Validity: the extent to which research gives a true and accurate picture of what it claims to measure. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “research population”, and give one example.
items.answer: The whole group that a researcher is interested in studying. Example: all secondary school teachers in a country.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the whole group that a researcher is interested in studying); 1 mark for a relevant example such as all secondary school teachers in a country. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “Hawthorne effect” and “interviewer bias”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Hawthorne effect: the tendency of people to change their behaviour because they know they are being studied (e.g. workers working harder because researchers are watching). Interviewer bias: the influence of the interviewer’s characteristics or behaviour on the answers given (e.g. respondents giving answers they think the interviewer wants).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Sofia studies 15 pupils from one school in Kathmandu and claims that the findings apply to all pupils in the country. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: research should be reliable and representative so that findings can be generalised and tested; standardised, large-scale methods such as questionnaires achieve this.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Ana studies 15 pupils from one school in Karachi and claims that the findings apply to all pupils in the country. Explain how a positivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Positivism: research should be reliable and representative so that findings can be generalised and tested; standardised, large-scale methods such as questionnaires achieve this.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Two researchers use the same structured interview schedule in Santiago and obtain very similar results. Explain how positivist and interpretivist sociologists might differ in the way they evaluate this research.
items.answer: Positivism: research should be reliable and representative so that findings can be generalised and tested; standardised, large-scale methods such as questionnaires achieve this. Interpretivism: validity matters most: the aim is to understand meanings and experiences in depth, even if samples are small and studies are hard to repeat.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful field experiments are for studying pupils’ attitudes to school.
items.answer: Strengths: variables in a school, such as teacher expectations, can be altered in a normal classroom; one variable can be altered (for example the name on a job application) to test its effect. Limitations: they are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change; the researcher has much less control over variables than in a laboratory. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying pupils’ attitudes to school but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying voting behaviour in a national election.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying voting behaviour in a national election but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “representativeness”.
items.answer: The extent to which a sample has the same characteristics as the wider population it is drawn from.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the extent to which a sample has the same characteristics as the wider population it is drawn from. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “interviewer bias” and “Hawthorne effect”?
items.answer: Interviewer bias: the influence of the interviewer’s characteristics or behaviour on the answers given. Hawthorne effect: the tendency of people to change their behaviour because they know they are being studied.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Which term describes issues such as time, money, access and the skills of the researcher that affect the choice of method?
items.answer: Practical factors
items.markingKey: Practical factors: issues such as time, money, access and the skills of the researcher that affect the choice of method. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “debriefing”, and give one example.
items.answer: Telling participants the true purpose of a study after it has finished, especially if deception was used. Example: explaining to participants that a field experiment was being carried out.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (telling participants the true purpose of a study after it has finished, especially if deception was used); 1 mark for a relevant example such as explaining to participants that a field experiment was being carried out. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “confidentiality” and “research aims”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Confidentiality: keeping the identities and information of research participants private (e.g. using pseudonyms in a published report). Research aims: the purposes of a study, which shape the type of data and methods needed (e.g. aiming to measure trends or to understand experiences).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A government department in Riyadh offers funding for research into youth unemployment but wants “hard statistics” for its report. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: sociology should study society scientifically, using quantitative, reliable methods such as questionnaires and official statistics to discover social facts, correlations and causes; the researcher should remain objective and detached (Comte, Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A government department in Colombo offers funding for research into youth unemployment but wants “hard statistics” for its report. Explain how a feminist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Feminism: research has often ignored women’s experiences; feminist researchers prefer non-hierarchical, qualitative methods that give women a voice and take account of power relationships in research (Oakley).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying the attitudes of senior managers in large companies.
items.answer: Strengths: they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the attitudes of senior managers in large companies but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Define the term “theoretical factors”.
items.answer: The influence of the researcher’s methodological perspective, such as positivism or interpretivism, on the choice of method.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the influence of the researcher’s methodological perspective, such as positivism or interpretivism, on the choice of method. [1]

items.stem: A sociologist in Lima wants to research young carers who look after a disabled parent. Explain one limitation of using unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: The power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of young carers who look after a disabled parent. [2]

items.stem: Which term describes a sampling method in which every member of the research population has an equal chance of being selected?
items.answer: Random sampling
items.markingKey: Random sampling: a sampling method in which every member of the research population has an equal chance of being selected. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “purposive sampling”? Give one example.
items.answer: Deliberately choosing participants because they have characteristics relevant to the research. Example: selecting only head teachers to study school leadership.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (deliberately choosing participants because they have characteristics relevant to the research); 1 mark for a relevant example such as selecting only head teachers to study school leadership. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “systematic sampling” and “random sampling”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Systematic sampling: selecting every nth person from a sampling frame (e.g. choosing every 10th name on an electoral roll). Random sampling: a sampling method in which every member of the research population has an equal chance of being selected (e.g. drawing names from a complete school register using a random number generator).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A researcher in Manila wants to interview undocumented migrant workers, who are afraid of being reported to the authorities. Suggest how an interpretivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: representativeness matters less than depth; small purposive or snowball samples are acceptable when the aim is to understand meanings in hard-to-reach groups.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Nairobi wants to interview undocumented migrant workers, who are afraid of being reported to the authorities. Explain how a positivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Positivism: sampling should be random and representative so that findings can be generalised to the whole population and tested statistically.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful unstructured interviews are for studying attitudes of university students to part-time work.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; the interviewee can raise issues the researcher had not thought of, so the research is not limited by pre-set categories. Limitations: they cannot measure patterns across a large population because only a few people can be interviewed; each interview is unique, so it is hard to repeat and the data is less reliable. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying attitudes of university students to part-time work but best combined with another method such as laboratory experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Chloe wants a stratified random sample of 150 from 1200 employees at a factory in Lisbon. The population is made up of 480 manual workers, 240 office workers, 480 managers. How many office workers should be in the sample?
Which term describes the view that sociologists must understand the subjective meanings people give to their actions, using qualitative methods?
items.answer: Interpretivism
items.markingKey: Interpretivism: the view that sociologists must understand the subjective meanings people give to their actions, using qualitative methods. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “interpretivism”.
items.answer: The view that sociologists must understand the subjective meanings people give to their actions, using qualitative methods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the view that sociologists must understand the subjective meanings people give to their actions, using qualitative methods. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “social facts” and “interpretivism”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Social facts: Durkheim’s term for social phenomena that exist outside individuals and constrain their behaviour (e.g. suicide rates, laws and religious norms). Interpretivism: the view that sociologists must understand the subjective meanings people give to their actions, using qualitative methods (e.g. a researcher joining a gang to understand members’ motives).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Kathmandu wants to research the experiences of homeless people in Auckland. Explain one limitation of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: The observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the experiences of homeless people in Auckland. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating why some young people leave school early. Explain two limitations of using semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule. 2. Interviewer bias may still affect answers.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to why some young people leave school early. [4]

items.stem: A researcher analysed 500 journal articles published in sociology journals and recorded the main methods used. Table: percentage of articles using | 2000 | 2025. Mainly quantitative methods | 51% | 40%. Mainly qualitative methods | 31% | 26%. Mixed methods | 18% | 34%. (a) Calculate the gap between Mainly quantitative methods and Mainly qualitative methods in 2000 and in 2025, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Explain one limitation of using content analysis to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the debate between positivism and interpretivism is less important today.
items.answer: (a) 2000: 20 percentage points; 2025: 14 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) Counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Mixed methods; the figure fell for Mainly quantitative methods, Mainly qualitative methods; Mainly quantitative methods had the highest figure for 2025. Mixed methods allow triangulation, improving validity and reliability. Qualifications: Most studies still rely mainly on one approach; theoretical preferences still shape choice of method; a sample of journals may not represent all research. The data also come from content analysis of 500 journal articles in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (20 and 14); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the extent to which research produces the same results when repeated by another researcher using the same method?
items.answer: Reliability
items.markingKey: Reliability: the extent to which research produces the same results when repeated by another researcher using the same method. [1]

items.stem: Briefly explain Oakley’s view that interviews should be non-hierarchical so that respondents are treated as equals.
items.answer: Oakley argued that a sympathetic, two-way interview with women produces more valid data than a detached, “masculine” interview.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Oakley argued that a sympathetic, two-way interview with women produces more valid data than a detached, “masculine” interview. [2]

items.stem: Aisha is planning a study of pupils’ attitudes to school. Explain one limitation of using field experiments for this research.
items.answer: They are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of pupils’ attitudes to school. [2]

items.stem: A research company recorded the response rates for 60 surveys it carried out in Muscat. Table: response rate | 2005 | 2025. Postal questionnaire | 35% | 26%. Online questionnaire | 31% | 30%. Face-to-face structured interview | 63% | 55%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Online questionnaire change between 2005 and 2025?
items.answer: -1 percentage point
items.markingKey: 30 − 31 = -1 percentage point. [1]

items.stem: Yusuf is planning a study of voting behaviour in a national election. Explain two limitations of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: 1. Sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time. 2. They are very expensive and results take many years to appear.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to voting behaviour in a national election. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using structured interviews to research domestic violence in Seoul.
items.answer: Strengths: every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable; the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled. Limitations: respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying domestic violence in Seoul but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.answer: Practical factors

items.stem: Explain Humphreys’s argument that covert observation can give access to hidden behaviour that people would never report, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Humphreys’s “Tearoom Trade” study of men in public toilets used covert observation and later traced participants to interview them in disguise. Criticism: It is widely criticised as unethical because it used deception and risked exposing participants.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Interactionism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Ravi, a student with a small budget and only three months, wants to study the experiences of refugees in Kathmandu. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: sociology should study society scientifically, using quantitative, reliable methods such as questionnaires and official statistics to discover social facts, correlations and causes; the researcher should remain objective and detached (Comte, Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Explain two ethical issues that may arise in sociological research.
items.answer: Informed consent; deception (covert methods); confidentiality and anonymity; harm to participants (psychological, legal, social); vulnerable groups such as children; harm to researchers; legal obligations to report crime.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Informed consent; deception (covert methods); confidentiality and anonymity; harm to participants (psychological, legal, social); vulnerable groups such as children; harm to researchers; legal obligations to report crime. [8]

items.stem: Define the term “quota sampling”.
items.answer: Selecting people who fit pre-set categories in proportion to the population until each quota is filled, without random selection.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: selecting people who fit pre-set categories in proportion to the population until each quota is filled, without random selection. [1]

items.stem: Savage argued that self-selecting online samples can produce biased pictures of the class structure. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: The Great British Class Survey attracted mainly educated, middle-class volunteers, so researchers had to add a separate nationally representative survey. Criticism: Defenders argue very large online samples can still reveal useful patterns.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Weberian theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Daniel is planning a study of attitudes of university students to part-time work. Explain one strength of using non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: The researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of attitudes of university students to part-time work. [2]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why sociologists may use non-random sampling methods.
items.answer: No sampling frame for hidden or deviant groups (snowball); cost and time (opportunity, quota); purposive aims in qualitative research; difficulty of access; interpretivist aims do not require representativeness.

items.answer: Closed questions impose the researcher’s categories.

items.stem: Explain Durkheim’s argument that suicide rates are social facts that can be explained by levels of social integration and regulation, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Durkheim used official statistics comparatively to show suicide rates varied with integration and regulation (egoistic, altruistic, anomic, fatalistic suicide). Criticism: Atkinson and Douglas argue suicide statistics are socially constructed by coroners’ judgements.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Positivism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A researcher analysed 200 journal articles published in sociology journals and recorded the main methods used. Table: percentage of articles using | 2000 | 2025. Mainly quantitative methods | 45% | 36%. Mainly qualitative methods | 32% | 28%. Mixed methods | 23% | 36%. (a) Calculate the gap between Mixed methods and Mainly qualitative methods in 2000 and in 2025, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of methods used in published sociological research. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the debate between positivism and interpretivism is less important today.
items.answer: (a) 2000: 9 percentage points; 2025: 8 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) Counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Mixed methods; the figure fell for Mainly quantitative methods, Mainly qualitative methods. Many sociologists now combine positivist and interpretivist approaches (methodological pluralism). Qualifications: Most studies still rely mainly on one approach; theoretical preferences still shape choice of method; a sample of journals may not represent all research. The data also come from content analysis of 200 journal articles in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (9 and 8); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the extent to which a sample has the same characteristics as the wider population it is drawn from?
items.answer: Representativeness
items.markingKey: Representativeness: the extent to which a sample has the same characteristics as the wider population it is drawn from. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “A reliable method always produces valid data.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. A method can give consistent results that are still inaccurate, e.g. a questionnaire where people give socially desirable answers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Arjun studies 15 pupils from one school in Kuala Lumpur and claims that the findings apply to all pupils in the country. Suggest how an interpretivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: validity matters most: the aim is to understand meanings and experiences in depth, even if samples are small and studies are hard to repeat.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: The table shows response rates for different survey methods, reported by a research agency in Karachi that ran 40 surveys. Table: response rate | 2005 | 2025. Postal questionnaire | 29% | 21%. Online questionnaire | 30% | 22%. Face-to-face structured interview | 69% | 57%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Postal questionnaire change between 2005 and 2025?
items.answer: -8 percentage points
items.markingKey: 21 − 29 = -8 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Arjun studies 15 pupils from one school in Lagos and claims that the findings apply to all pupils in the country. Explain how an interpretivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: validity matters most: the aim is to understand meanings and experiences in depth, even if samples are small and studies are hard to repeat.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) to research voting behaviour in a national election.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; they can combine quantitative and qualitative data. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying voting behaviour in a national election but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes moral issues about the way research affects the people involved, such as consent, harm and confidentiality?
items.answer: Ethical factors
items.markingKey: Ethical factors: moral issues about the way research affects the people involved, such as consent, harm and confidentiality. [1]

items.stem: Explain two practical factors that may influence a sociologist’s choice of research method.
items.answer: Time: participant observation may take months or years; cost: national surveys or trained interviewers are expensive; access: some groups (e.g. elites or gangs) are hard to reach; researcher characteristics: age, gender or ethnicity may affect access; funding bodies may want quantitative data.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained factor. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating people who have experienced homelessness in Accra. Explain one limitation of using semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of people who have experienced homelessness in Accra. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of laboratory experiments for studying young carers who look after a disabled parent.
items.answer: Strengths: the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability; results are quantitative and easy to compare. Limitations: it would be unethical to recreate harmful situations, such as violence, in a laboratory; the artificial setting means people may not behave as they would in real life, so validity is low. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying young carers who look after a disabled parent but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: State one reason why researchers may not be able to use random sampling.
items.answer: Those selected may refuse to take part.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. those selected may refuse to take part. [1]

items.stem: Explain one strength and one limitation of opportunity sampling.
items.answer: Strength: quick, cheap and easy. Limitation: those available (e.g. shoppers on a weekday morning) are unlikely to represent the population, so findings cannot be generalised.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each explained point. [4]

items.stem: Sofia wants a stratified random sample of 80 from 1600 adults in a town near Kathmandu. The population is made up of 560 aged 18-34, 320 aged 35-59, 720 aged 60 and over. Calculate the number from each group needed in the sample.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for all 3 correct values summing to 80. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying drug use among young people in Lima.
items.answer: Strengths: anonymity may encourage respondents to admit sensitive or embarrassing behaviour they would not reveal face to face; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying drug use among young people in Lima but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
